h: Who is the anarchist: the young people packed into buses, or the government?
dek: Dilip Khan tests the word 'anarchist' against its philosophical meaning and asks who actually brought the city to a standstill on 10 October.
photo_note: A photograph from the Delhi march. The placard carries an allegation against the Election Commission; that is what the photo shows, not Deshkaal's conclusion.
ank: metro stations shut (according to the author)
when Proudhon called himself an anarchist in 'What Is Property?'
body: As Delhi Police buses carried thousands of protesters towards stadiums on the edge of the city, BJP spokesperson Sambit Patra called them 'anarchic elements' and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta said the capital would not be held hostage. Dilip Khan begins with that word. In his view 'anarchist' is an accusation that never has to be proved. Stick it on any crowd or slogan and the argument ends right there.

His case is that the word quietly assumes the present arrangement is the only one possible. If a young person who questions names being struck off the voter list is an anarchist, he asks, who gave the arrangement that strikes the names off the status of 'order'? According to Khan, these protests had no fixed leader. Neither the 20 July protest nor the one on 10 October was led by a single organisation. Anarchist thought sees that as strength, not weakness.

He then moves to Proudhon, Kropotkin and Bhagat Singh's 1928 series of articles, and explains the difference between order and control. Silence born of fear is control. Order is where people can disagree without being afraid. To Ambedkar's 'grammar of anarchy' argument, his reply is that the condition that constitutional routes must actually be open is often left out.

Khan claims the city was brought to a halt more by the arrangements to stop the protest than by the protest itself. According to him, 57 metro stations were closed, trains were stopped and thousands were detained. He reminds readers that the Supreme Court had said a day earlier that metro and rail should not be fully shut. He also writes that in Connaught Place, men carrying lathis beat protesters in front of the police, and that action came only after the video went viral.

In the end his argument rests on selective enforcement. Deciding whom the law applies to and whom it spares is itself arbitrary rule. When rules start to apply depending on whether the person in front is with power or against it, the trust between citizen and state begins to break.
nazar: Khan's most useful question is who carries the burden of proof. A protester must prove his intent first in an application, then on the train, then in detention, while nobody asks those in power why the internet was cut. The burden of saving one's name on the voter list also falls on the ordinary person.

Many of the essay's claims rest on the author's own testimony: the closure of 57 stations, the detention counts, the police's role in the Connaught Place beating and the account of the Supreme Court's remarks. The police and the government may tell a different story, so until they respond it is fair to read these as allegations. Accountability for mob violence matters just as much, whichever side it comes from.
sawal: If rules are applied by choice, whose law is it?
ref: Pyotr Kropotkin
Russian thinker and anarchist. His book 'Mutual Aid' argues that cooperation matters more than competition in the survival of species and societies.
Pierre-Joseph Proudhon
French thinker who called himself an anarchist in his 1840 book 'What Is Property?'. He favoured an order built on mutual exchange over commands imposed from above.

h: March reaches the Supreme Court as the Commission stands firm
dek: Al Jazeera, AFP and Reuters: for a third day thousands of police stayed deployed, yet crowds of opposition supporters and young people reached the roads around the Supreme Court.
photo_note: An aerial view of a crowd gathered with flags. Independent confirmation of place and time is pending.
body: Al Jazeera recorded Monday's march using reports from international news agencies. According to it, thousands of people reached the roads leading to the Supreme Court, shouting slogans. The demand remained the same: Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar must resign.

The report says thousands of police and security personnel were deployed in central Delhi for a third straight day, heavy metal barricades were set up and half a dozen metro stations were closed. Rahul Gandhi had called for the march. Citing his post on X addressed to Home Minister Amit Shah, the report says he is not someone who will be scared or step back.

The outlet counts two streams in the movement: opposition parties, and a youth movement called the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), said to have millions of social media followers. According to the report, thousands of protesters were detained last weekend. CPM MP John Brittas alleged that police dragged and assaulted him. The police did not respond to these questions.

The Election Commission's side is also recorded. The Commission has denied any wrongdoing and said the revision of the voter list was meant to remove duplicate, dead and fake names. Citing media reports, the report says more than 13.3 crore (133 million) names were removed in the process. Critics allege the impact fell more heavily on minorities, especially Muslims.
nazar: Even in the language of international agencies this is no longer one party's rally; it is counted as the biggest political challenge in 12 years of the Modi government. That is the reporter's assessment, not Deshkaal's conclusion.
The figure of 13.3 crore comes from 'media reports' and has not been separately verified. The claim about impact is the critics', and the Commission denies it. Both sides are worth reading together.
sawal: When the questions are for the Commission, why is the police answering on the street?
ref: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)
A youth movement named in the report, said to have millions of followers on social media.
Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the voter list
The Election Commission's process of checking the list and adding or removing names.

h: How can anyone trust this Election Commission?
dek: Sanjay Dubey in Satyagrah: put two election commissioners' written objections, the change to Form 6 and the appointment law side by side, and the questions are for the Commission, not the police.
body: Sanjay Dubey's opening point is simple: the protests in Delhi are peaceful, yet people are not being allowed even near Jantar Mantar. He asks why the police are answering questions put to the Election Commission, when the Commission itself stays silent and BJP spokespersons or the chief minister reply.

The essay rests on a September 2026 Indian Express report whose basic points, according to the author, the Commission has not denied. According to it, Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi recorded written objections at least 14 times between November 2025 and September 2026. They called the addition of the earlier-SIR question to Form 6 'illegal' and 'unauthorised'. The report also records that for about four months the three commissioners did not hold a joint meeting, and that both wrote separately to the Cabinet Secretary. The Commission's reply was only that the letters concerned the working of one official.

The author cites the West Bengal figures: about 60 lakh people received notices over discrepancies; of those whom judicial officers kept on the list, appeals against about 16 lakh were filed by the Commission itself; and the Commission told the Supreme Court about 38 lakh tribunal cases in all, but not that it had filed 16 lakh of them. This is the author's conclusion, drawn from the report.

The second part concerns appointments. In March 2023 a five-judge Supreme Court bench gave an interim arrangement of a selection committee that included the Chief Justice; a law of December 2023 removed him. After Arun Goel's resignation, the appointments of Gyanesh Kumar and Sandhu came just before a Supreme Court hearing. The author says plainly that these events do not prove the Commission is in league with the government, but that putting them together and asking questions cannot be dismissed.
nazar: The strength of the essay is that it offers fewer accusations and more recorded documents. The weak link is that the proof of the commissioners' objections rests on one newspaper report, not yet confirmed by an official account from the Commission.
The conclusion that 'the Commission misled the court' is the author's. Neither the court nor the Commission has said any such thing.
sawal: If two members of the Commission object in writing and the public stays silent, what kind of trust is that?
ref: Form 6
The application filled in to add a new voter's name to the list.
ERO
Electoral Registration Officer, usually an SDM, who holds the legal authority to decide on the voter list.

h: 146 lawyers, 7,000 detentions and four directions from the court
dek: Zoom News: Delhi Police accused of ignoring the Supreme Court's 9 October order; the bench of Justice Bagchi and Justice Mohana issued notice and sought a reply by 13 October.
photo_note: A crowd and parked buses. Independent confirmation of date and place is pending.
body: According to Zoom News, 146 lawyers appeared together in the Supreme Court against Delhi Police and the administration, alleging that the court's order of 9 October had been ignored. The special hearing was before a bench of Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana.

Senior advocate Menaka Guruswamy, according to the report, told the court that about 7,000 people had been unlawfully detained. The petitioners claimed more than 45 metro stations were closed, restrictions were placed at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin railway stations, and the internet was cut. They also argued that notice boards under Section 163 of the BNSS around the Supreme Court obstructed the movement of lawyers, journalists and ordinary people. Several senior lawyers appeared, including K. Venugopal, Kapil Sibal, Gopal Sankaranarayanan, Sanjay Hegde and Shadan Farasat.
For the government, V. Raju denied the allegations. He said that only 45 of Delhi's 303 metro stations were closed temporarily and later reopened, and that internet services are restored.

According to the report, the bench issued notice to the officials concerned, sought a detailed reply by 13 October and directed that: the metro and internet run normally, peaceful protesters not be unlawfully detained, the Section 163 boards be removed from outside the Supreme Court, and lawyers and journalists not be stopped from working. The next hearing is on 13 October.
nazar: This is not the court's final verdict but interim directions and a notice. The figure of 7,000 detentions is the petitioners' argument, not the court's finding. The government's count (45 of 303) is separate.
The report gives the hearing date as 11 October, while the story is dated 12 October. We are waiting for a copy of the order to confirm the date.
sawal: The reply is due tomorrow; until then, who will watch whether the order is followed?
ref: BNSS Section 163
A prohibitory order that bars people from gathering in an area; it replaces the earlier Section 144.
Interim directions
An order the court gives before its final judgment to handle the immediate situation.

h: 'This is a tandav, it has no plan': Rahul Gandhi's attack
dek: The Week: an open warning to the Chief Election Commissioner, an announced petition in the Supreme Court and a claim that 200 government officials are in touch, all in Rahul Gandhi's own words.
body: According to The Week, Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi said at a press conference before the march that Gyanesh Kumar 'cannot sleep at night' and 'will not survive as Chief Election Commissioner'. He divided the struggle into two sides: the public and the opposition on one, and Narendra Modi, Amit Shah, Ajit Doval and Gyanesh Kumar on the other.

Rahul Gandhi said he and Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge had written to Chief Justice Surya Kant. In his words, the Chief Justice replied asking them to file a petition. On that basis, India bloc leaders were to reach the Supreme Court the same day. According to Zoom News headlines, the petition by 11 leaders seeks the Chief Election Commissioner's resignation.

He also made a separate claim, that about 200 officials of the Modi government are in touch with the opposition and sharing information. The report gives no details or evidence for this claim. The charges that Delhi has been turned into a 'fortress' and that people are being stopped from reaching it are also his.

His answer on the question of planning is recorded in the report: his sister Priyanka asks him to plan, but this is 'Shiva's tandav', the Supreme Court today, something else tomorrow. The march was fixed to start at 1.30 pm from Barakhamba crossing.
nazar: Phrases like '200 officials' and 'five criminals' are Rahul Gandhi's political statements, not facts. No reply from Gyanesh Kumar or the Election Commission is recorded in this report.
What the petition asks and what the court says will become clear only after the hearing. The details of the letter to the Chief Justice and his reply also come only from Rahul Gandhi's statement.
sawal: A claim with no evidence offered: news, or a slogan?
ref: Leader of the Opposition
The leader of the largest opposition party in the Lok Sabha, who sits on the selection committees for constitutional posts.

h: 'Jantar Mantar is gone, not the protest': Akhilesh at the protest site
dek: Aaj Tak: Akhilesh Yadav, who joined the walk to the Supreme Court, said changing the venue will not stop the fight. According to The Tribune's headline, Ramlila Maidan is free for only three dates till year-end.
body: According to Aaj Tak, India bloc leaders were marching on foot to the Supreme Court over the voter list dispute, and Samajwadi Party president Akhilesh Yadav joined them. His statement became the headline: Jantar Mantar is gone, not the protest, and wherever we sit will be our dharna.

The report says he questioned the change of protest venue and said it would not stop the opposition's struggle. He also repeated the demand for the Chief Election Commissioner's resignation. We could not read the full text, so only what is in the report's introduction is recorded here.

The question of venue matters because over the past week police did not let protesters go even near Jantar Mantar. A headline in The Tribune says only three dates are open for protests at Ramlila Maidan till year-end, and a day's booking costs Rs 1.21 lakh. We could not read the original text of that story, so reliance on the details is limited to the headline.
Put side by side, the two things raise the question that was also raised in court: how much access to a designated place for peaceful protest is left, and who will pay its price.
nazar: Akhilesh Yadav's statement is political, but it holds a concrete question: who decides the place of protest, the police or the law?
We have taken the Ramlila Maidan dates and rent figure from the headline alone. It will be updated as soon as we confirm it by reading the story directly.
sawal: If you are not allowed to reach the designated place, where does protest go?
ref: Jantar Mantar
The area of New Delhi that has been the designated place for sit-ins and protests for decades.

h: Statements from over 20 journalists: showed press cards, put on a bus anyway
dek: The News Minute and Scroll reports, on Newslaundry: journalists were detained, cameras broken and phones snatched even after the Supreme Court's 11 October direction.
body: The News Minute spoke to about 20 journalists, most from digital media. According to the report, on 10 and 11 October they were detained, beaten, threatened and had their equipment snatched or broken. All this happened even after the Supreme Court's direction of the afternoon of 11 October that lawyers, journalists and other professionals must not be obstructed in their work in any way.

The accounts come from different places. One journalist said that in Connaught Place he was put on a bus and beaten, and policemen jabbed the butt of a gun into his stomach. When he cited the court order, the police laughed it off. One cameraman said his lens was broken, the battery and memory card went missing, and he was taken as far as Zafrabad police station. Several journalists said that when they showed press cards they were told anyone can get a card made and only PIB card holders would be spared.

Some accounts mention right-wing groups in the crowd who identified journalists and signalled to the police. One journalist was freed from detention when a lawyer read out the court's order. In several cases officers at DCP level instructed that people be released on the spot, and one expressed regret.

The report ends with a remark that is news in itself: one journalist said that for the first time in his life he had to hide his camera and press card in his bag. According to the report, Molitics' Instagram account, which had 5.67 lakh followers, was withdrawn in India for 'legal reasons'.
nazar: These are journalists' personal accounts and the police's side is not in the report. According to a separate Scroll report, Delhi Police have been asked for a response. The allegations against named officers are those journalists' own.

When a reporter is put on a bus, there is one fewer person making the news and one more person who is part of it. When a journalist has to hide a press card instead of a camera, the loss is not only the journalist's.
sawal: What is it that the one who will not let the camera see is hiding?
ref: PIB card
An identity card given by the government's Press Information Bureau to accredited journalists.

h: The court said obey the law, but did not ask what the law permits
dek: Sarthak Gupta and Prannv Dhawan in Scroll: what law gives the power to stop a protest before it begins, and what evidence does it need?
body: The two lawyers set the Supreme Court's orders out in sequence. The order of 9 October called the metro closures and train cancellations 'excessive', but its words were soft: the Solicitor General agreed to 'persuade' the authorities and the court hoped for 'prudent decisions'. According to the authors, an assurance differs from a direction, because under an assurance the decision stays in the government's hands.

The facts recorded in the essay: police asked for 57 metro stations to be closed, Railways cancelled more than 250 mail and express trains, and according to the Solicitor General movement was restricted at 45 of 303 stations. Figures on detentions differ: more than 2,500 to 3,000 citing police, about 7,000 according to lawyers.

The authors' main argument is that a few hours of detention end before any court can examine them. Release ends the detention but does not settle whether it was lawful. They remind readers that on 1 September the court used Article 142 to quash 129 FIRs from the NEET protest, but did not decide whether the protest was lawful.

The sharpest question is about permission. According to the authors, Justice Bagchi's remark at the 9 October hearing, that a protest without permission is not in accordance with law, inverts the constitutional starting point. Under the 2018 MKSS judgment, regulation must be reasonable and proportionate: state the concrete risk, show how the measure relates to it, and explain why less restrictive options were not tried.
nazar: This is opinion, not a ruling. The authors quote Justice Bagchi's remark from reports, and not everything a court says is an order.

After the essay, the question before the court today is plain: in its reply, will the government place the legal basis and evidence for the restrictions? The government's reply is due at Tuesday's hearing.
sawal: If the court gives an order, why should its effect not show on the day of the protest itself?
ref: Article 142
The provision that empowers the Supreme Court to pass orders to do 'complete justice'.
Habeas corpus
A writ ordering that a detained person be produced before the court and the grounds for detention be stated.

h: The right to vote is citizenship itself, which is why this protest did not bend to pressure
dek: Neera Chandhoke in The Wire: a generation that cast its first vote at 21 is now asked to prove it is a citizen. For the author, that is the root of the anger.
body: Neera Chandhoke, a former professor of political science at Delhi University, begins with a personal memory: in 1968, when free India and her generation both turned 21, voting gave her the feeling of being a citizen. That same generation is now being asked to prove its claim to citizenship, which she sees as both 'brazenness' and a calculated move.

She alleges that SIR pushed people off the list on a large scale, including Amartya Sen, and the estimate is that 13 crore names were removed. The essay gives no source for these figures. According to the author, the aim is to exclude voters who are not the ruling party's support base, and she puts this allegation in the language of 'it is said', citing 'many capable observers'.

She then explains why the movement did not give in to pressure. Trains were stopped, barricades set up and metro stations shut, yet people reached Delhi on foot. In her argument, the right to vote grants membership of a political community, and one who sees that membership being taken away also exercises the right to question, protest and disobey.

The essay cites Jantar Mantar on 20 July, where, according to her, masked men attacked protesters with sticks and rods, and mentions excesses against women. It ends with Brecht's line: would it not be easier for the government to dissolve the people and elect another?
nazar: This essay is more anger and moral appeal than argument. Its strength lies in reminding us of the link between citizenship and the vote; its weakness is that the basis for claims like 13 crore and 'excluding only one community' is not found in it.
The Election Commission's argument is that the revision removed duplicate, dead and fake names. That side is not in the essay and the reader will have to read it separately.
sawal: If the citizen must give proof, when will the government have to give proof?
ref: SIR
Special Intensive Revision: the Election Commission's process of checking the voter list house to house and adding or removing names.
Brecht
The German poet and playwright Bertolt Brecht, whose 1953 poem 'The Solution' has the famous line about dissolving the people.

h: The street has delivered its verdict: a day on the ground in Delhi
dek: Sanjay K. Jha in The Wire: amid tired slogans on Barakhamba Road a drum suddenly sounded and the mood of the crowd changed. The author reads it as a warning to the government.
body: Political commentator Sanjay K. Jha writes the scene of Monday. From 12 noon the crowd walked along Barakhamba Road, and by four it was tired, the slogans had turned repetitive. Then drums sounded, a cry of 'He has come, he has come' rose, and Rahul Gandhi arrived. The police and paramilitary, who in his words had been writing the headlines of recent days, stood as spectators on both sides.

The essay has quotes from ordinary people: a woman from Karol Bagh whose two sons are unemployed, a cloth trader ready to 'come every day for months', a retired government employee. The author himself admits that Congress mobilised its MLAs and MPs and they came in buses, yet he still calls it 'the verdict of the street'.

His conclusion is that it is not only opposition unity: ordinary people are seeing vote theft as a moral decline. He also writes that Rahul Gandhi himself said it would be wrong to expect quick results and that people should be ready for a long fight.

At the end the author adds a list of old grievances: the promise of Rs 15 lakh, unemployment, inflation, then 'donation theft' and 'vote theft'. This whole list is one commentator's interpretation, not the result of any survey.
nazar: This is not ground reporting but a piece that takes a side. The size of the crowd is not given in figures in the essay. Another report in The Wire, citing a Congress member, estimates 40,000 to 50,000, while Zoom News wrote 'hundreds' of supporters.
The gap shows that every side counts in its own way. Nobody yet has an independent figure.
sawal: Who has the job of counting the crowd, when everyone has their own figures?
ref: Chanda chori (donation theft)
A phrase used in the essay for allegations about political donations. It is the author's political idiom.

h: Permanent instability in the Gulf: old alliances are no longer a shield
dek: Nesrine Malik in The Guardian: the Houthi attack on the Saudi capital exposed the Gulf's vulnerability. For the author, trusting the American security umbrella is now a wrong bet.
body: Nesrine Malik's essay begins with Saturday's attack. According to her, a Houthi missile attack killed at least 13 people and injured 300 at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. According to the essay, after the US and Israeli attack on Iran in February, this is the deadliest attack on any Gulf country.

Her argument is that over the past year the Gulf's 'sacred safe' status has broken. Iranian missiles on Qatar, an Israeli attack on Doha, and then, in the war with Iran, Iranian attacks on Bahrain, Kuwait, the UAE, Oman, Qatar and Saudi Arabia, targeting military sites, energy and water purification plants. Schools stayed shut for months and airports came to a halt.

The Yemen part is separate. According to the essay, the closure of Hormuz diverted ships towards Yemen's coast, the Houthis expanded territory to control Bab al-Mandab, and Saudi action intensified. The author does not see the Houthis as merely Iran's pawns; they have their own ambitions and an old enmity with the Saudi royal family.

The last argument is that last month the Trump administration refused to give Saudi Arabia military help in fighting the Houthis. According to the author, this let both ally and enemy see the limits of the American umbrella.
nazar: This is an opinion essay and the death toll is as of the author's writing. The official figure and the Saudi government's side are not in the essay.
For India this is not distant news. Instability in the Gulf means oil prices, the safety of migrant workers and the impact on remittances, on which this essay says nothing.
sawal: If the promise of protection is someone else's, who are they relying on for their safety?
ref: Houthis
An Iran-backed armed group in Yemen that has held the capital Sanaa since 2014.
Bab al-Mandab
The narrow waterway of the Red Sea through which a large share of maritime trade passes.

h: Fewer rules than a fridge: a call for international law on AI
dek: Richard Hermer, former UK Attorney General, in The Guardian: the danger from AI is existential, and self-regulation cannot handle it.
body: Richard Hermer was the UK's Attorney General for two years. He says that even after doing the most work on national security in those two years, he finds the AI danger of a different kind, because the window of time for it is limited.

He splits the danger into two. First, existential risk: AI could make tasks like building biological weapons easier, or could decide on its own that humans are unnecessary. Second, an existential challenge: if left uncontrolled, billions of people will lose control over their lives, and power will be concentrated in a few countries and a few individuals.

His comparison is direct. A company making toasters would not be allowed to sell a product with a 10 per cent chance of electric shock, yet AI labs have fewer rules than a fridge. He says companies and markets are driven to bring out new versions quickly, so leaving regulation to the industry is laughable.

As a solution he speaks of international law, dialogue with the US and China, a coalition of like-minded countries and public debate. 'We cannot leave this to China, America and the big tech companies' is his core message.
nazar: The author himself accepts that nobody knows the true scale of the risk. A claim like 'the death of billions' is a warning, not a measured estimate.

Interestingly, the centre of the debate is still the US, China and Britain. Where countries like India, where AI use is growing in both employment and surveillance, would sit at this table is something the essay does not ask.
sawal: If a technology has fewer rules than a fridge, whose hands hold its decisions?
ref: Frontier AI
The most advanced and largest models, which only a few labs can build.

h: With Hamas or without it: the real question about Gaza's future
dek: An essay in Al Jazeera's opinion section: Hamas's future matters, but settling it does not solve Gaza's problem, because the roots lie in 1948 and the occupation.
body: The essay is written at the start of the war's fourth year. According to it, demands that Hamas give up governance and leave Gaza are growing louder, but the author argues that no solution will emerge without touching the conditions that gave birth to Hamas. He lists the villages emptied in 1948, the occupation of 1967 and the first intifada of 1987.

The essay cites Hamas's three founders, who came from families displaced in 1948. At the same time it plainly accepts that the attack of 7 October 2023 was Hamas's 'fatal decision'. It is not excused as a compulsion of history but placed in context.

The author separates two things. One, Hamas's action and the wishes of the Palestinian people. He cites a 2023 Arab Barometer survey, according to which only 29 per cent of Gazans trusted Hamas's government, 54 per cent favoured a two-state solution and 20 per cent favoured military action. Two, Hamas's presence and Gaza's destruction. In his view Hamas's presence cannot justify attacks on this scale.

At the end he lists the imbalance in the ceasefire talks: the Palestinian side faces conditions of recognition and renouncing violence, Israel does not. In his view Israel's demand for Hamas's complete disarmament closes the way to an agreement.
nazar: This is a one-sided opinion and Israel's reply is not in it. The survey figures are from before October 2023, so wartime public sentiment is not in them.
Even so, the essay's central question is valid: if removing an armed organisation leaves the question of occupation, how will peace come?
sawal: When the cause remains, what changes by removing one organisation?
ref: Nakba
The word used for the mass displacement of Palestinians in 1948, meaning 'catastrophe'.
Intifada
A Palestinian popular uprising against the occupation; the first intifada began in 1987.

h: Beaten in the van, phones snatched, released 40 km away: statements of detained protesters
dek: Scroll report: protesters picked up from central Delhi on Sunday were driven around for hours and taken to Pandwala Khurd in Najafgarh. Delhi Police's response is yet to come.
body: The van carrying Noreen, detained from central Delhi on Sunday afternoon, held 17 protesters, 15 of them women. According to Noreen, they were taken inside and beaten one by one. She alleged that Aranya of the Disha Students' Organisation was laid across the van door, throttled and elbowed. Aranya has also alleged beating in custody and said she will go to court.

Scroll spoke to people from two vans. Several said their phones were taken the moment they were put in. Lawyer and activist Arjun Unnikrishnan wrote on X that when a fellow detainee would not give his password he was slapped and his gallery was searched. It was said there were four minors in the van.

Around seven the van entered a community centre in Pandwala Khurd (Najafgarh), 40 km away. Lawyers who reached outside were not allowed in. Around 11.30 pm all were released, but phones were not returned. According to one protester, they were told to go home without money or phones.

Supreme Court Advocate-on-Record Soutik Banerjee told Scroll that the police have the power to clear a crowd, but the law does not give them the right to take people far away without the formal process of preventive detention.
nazar: These allegations are statements by protesters, and by the time of publication Delhi Police had not replied. Scroll has said the report will be updated when a reply comes.
According to the report, these incidents came a few hours after the Supreme Court's direction to avoid unlawful detention of peaceful protesters.
sawal: If the lawyer cannot see the place of detention, who holds its record?
ref: Preventive detention
A precautionary step taken without trial for a limited time on fear of a breach of peace, for which legal procedure and written grounds are required.

h: BJP's side: Shivraj Chouhan calls the march 'theatrics', Anurag Thakur says 'false allegations'
dek: Deccan Chronicle report: the Union minister accused Congress of weakening institutions and of harming the country's image with 'vote theft' allegations.
body: According to Deccan Chronicle, Union Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said on Monday that Congress wants to return to power by weakening constitutional institutions. He described the movement against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar as a crowd spreading anarchy on the streets.

Chouhan called Rahul Gandhi's march towards the Supreme Court 'theatrics'. His argument was that the reason for electoral defeat is not the Election Commission but Congress's leadership. On the attempt to meet the Chief Justice, he said there is a set procedure and it is not right to turn up any time by writing a letter.

Rahul Gandhi had called the movement 'Shiva's baraat'. Chouhan objected to this. He also alleged that Congress is playing into the hands of foreign forces. The report gives no fact or evidence in support of this allegation.

Former Union Minister Anurag Thakur said Rahul Gandhi keeps questioning the mandate by repeating 'vote theft' and is putting the blame for defeat on the Election Commission, EVMs and the Chief Election Commissioner. He called these allegations 'baseless'.
nazar: This is the ruling side's reaction and both leaders' statements are allegations. The basis of the 'foreign forces' claim is not given in the report.

The report has no factual reply from the Commission or the government on the core questions raised in the statements, that is, names struck off in the revision of the voter list and the commissioners' objections.
sawal: If an allegation is answered with an allegation, who will answer the question?
ref: Vote chori (vote theft)
The opposition's allegation that the voter list and electoral process were manipulated. The Election Commission and BJP reject it.

h: CJI says 'this is not my issue'; declines to meet the opposition, gives no reason
dek: According to Deccan Chronicle, Chief Justice Surya Kant declined to comment on Delhi's restrictions, but said the court's doors are open to everyone.
body: Asked by journalists at the 33rd foundation day function of the National Human Rights Commission, Chief Justice Surya Kant said, 'This is not my issue.' On the opposition's march towards the Supreme Court, he said he would not say anything.

Mallikarjun Kharge and Rahul Gandhi had asked for a meeting between 4 and 5 pm on Monday. Their demands were: a stop to alleged 'vote theft', the Chief Election Commissioner's resignation, a halt to SIR and the return of paper ballots. The CJI said he had sent a reply to the letter and stated the reasons for being unable to meet, but kept that reply confidential.

On the question of continuing protests, he said the Supreme Court's doors are open to all: 'whether a common man or a member of an elected body', every citizen has the right to approach the court and matters will be heard in accordance with law.

According to the report, 45 metro stations were closed at the weekend, checks at the borders were stepped up and thousands of protesters, including four former chief ministers, were detained. On declining to meet a Joint Committee of Parliament, the CJI also said there was a possibility of conflict of interest.
nazar: These are remarks made in conversation with journalists, not a court order. The directions of 11 October and Tuesday's hearing are separate things.
The CJI has not made public the reason for the meeting not taking place. So any guess about it is only a guess.
sawal: If the court's doors are open, who closed the way to reach them?
ref: Conflict of interest
When someone's personal or institutional interest may get in the way of their impartial role.

h: Over 100 billion units of renewable power in one quarter, but coal stock only 36 per cent
dek: CREA report in Down To Earth: peak demand hit a record 270 GW in the September quarter, yet coal plants ran at 68 per cent capacity.
body: According to the latest report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), power generation in the second quarter of 2026-27 rose 11 per cent to 536 billion units. Renewable generation, excluding large hydro, went above 100 billion units for the first time. Solar generation rose 39 per cent to 51 billion units and wind 29 per cent to 45 billion units.
Even so, coal and lignite, at 351 billion units, remained about 66 per cent of total generation. On 16 July demand hit a record 270 GW, 18 per cent more than the same quarter a year earlier.

Pressure showed in coal supply. On 30 September power stations had 21 million tonnes of coal left, against a normative requirement of 58 million tonnes. The number of plants with stock below 25 per cent of the norm rose from 32 on 22 August to 85 on 1 October.

According to CREA analyst Manoj Kumar, even at record demand coal plants were used at only 68 per cent, so new thermal capacity should be judged by looking at demand, renewable generation and storage. According to the report, 44 GW of coal capacity is still under construction.
nazar: These are CREA's figures, said to be based on data from Grid-India, the Ministry of Coal and the Central Electricity Authority. CREA is a research organisation that advocates clean energy.
The report also says that in July-August 1,835 million units of renewable power were wasted because of grid constraints.
sawal: When power is being made from the sun, for what demand are the new coal plants?
ref: Plant load factor
How much of its maximum capacity a power station actually produced.

h: Lucknow's flood was 'man-made': settlements drowned even at 25,000 cusecs
dek: Venkatesh Dutta's argument in Down To Earth: because the Gomti's floodplain and drains were encroached upon, even a modest flow became a flood.
body: According to the author, the October 2026 flood came not from Lucknow's rain but from rain in Pilibhit, Lakhimpur Kheri, Shahjahanpur and Sitapur. On 7 October the Gomti's flow was about 25,000 cusecs and the water level at Hanuman Setu about a metre below the warning level, yet low-lying settlements went under. The essay speaks of more than 1 lakh people affected and 40,000 houses partly submerged.

For comparison he recalls the flood of 1894, when the flow was 2.34 lakh cusecs, about ten times this time. He says dams, riverfront projects, roads and encroachment on ponds and tanks have shrunk the space for the river. According to his studies, more than 70 per cent of Lucknow's ponds and lakes are encroached upon.

He asks why the city is becoming dependent on pumping water out. The Lucknow Development Authority has proposed 12 more pumping stations. In his words, first we block the path of the water, then we spend money to pump it out.

He has also voiced concern over the Jal Shakti Ministry's 7 August 2026 Ganga Authority (Second Amendment) order, which added the category of 'active flood zone' and removed the reference to a 'no-construction zone'. He demands legal protection for the remaining ponds, wetlands and drains.
nazar: This is an opinion essay and Venkatesh Dutta's own analysis. The newspaper has stated plainly that the views are the author's. The Lucknow Development Authority's side is not in it.

In the essay he says the areas inundated at this water level lie in the river's khadar zone, where water has filled from time to time. That difference also opens the question of why settlements were built there.
sawal: Having hemmed in the river's path, why do we blame the rain for floods?
ref: Cusec
A unit of water flow: one cubic foot per second.
Khadar
The low land along a river that often goes under in floods.

h: News of Parvez Parwaz's death: Ajit Sahi's post and the 2020 report
dek: Ajit Sahi, citing Rajeev Yadav, has reported the death in Gorakhpur jail of Parvez Parwaz, who filed the hate speech case against Yogi Adityanath. We have found no official confirmation.
body: Journalist Ajit Sahi has written on social media that he learned from Rajeev Yadav that Parvez Parwaz has died in Gorakhpur jail. We found no confirmation of the date or cause of death or from the jail administration, so for now this is information supplied by Sahi.

According to Sahi, Parwaz filed a case in January 2007 over Adityanath's alleged speech in Gorakhpur. Sahi alleges that the governments of Mulayam Singh Yadav, Mayawati and Akhilesh Yadav tried to bury the case. Sahi wrote that he first met Parwaz in 2017 and last in 2019 in Allahabad.

The Wire's 2020 report records that the Gorakhpur district court had sentenced Parwaz to life imprisonment in a 2018 gang rape case. The complainant was a Muslim woman. Parwaz's friends and lawyers told the reporter he was framed, while the prosecution lawyer had said the proceedings were according to law.

According to the same report, in 2017 the High Court rebuked the state government over the failure to grant prosecution sanction in the hate speech case. Later the then Chief Secretary said the Home Department had not granted sanction, treating the CB-CID report as having insufficient evidence. The High Court found no lapse in procedure and the petition was dismissed.
nazar: The claims of murder, government pressure, corrupt judges and the change of investigating officer are Ajit Sahi's allegations. Deshkaal has not verified them independently. The death cannot be written as an established murder.

The conviction is a court's decision and the lawyer had spoken of an appeal against it. We did not find the later court position. The Uttar Pradesh government's or jail administration's side is not available.
sawal: When someone dies in jail, whose inquiry should come first?
ref: Prosecution sanction
The permission taken from the government before prosecuting a person holding a public post in certain cases.

h: Garm Hava: when a man was told to prove his place
dek: M.S. Sathyu's 1973 film is the story of a Muslim shoe manufacturer in Agra who wants to stay in his city even after Partition. It is worth watching again in today's SIR era.
body: In this film based on a story by Ismat Chughtai, Balraj Sahni plays Salim Mirza, a shoe manufacturer in Agra whose family leaves for Pakistan one by one in the years after Partition. Salim Mirza stays on, because this city is his. It was Farooq Shaikh's first major screen role.

The film does not show a big catastrophe. It counts small things: a bank loan stopped, a rented house not found, standing in the trade falling, and everywhere the suspicion of where their loyalty lies. More than drama, it trusts silence and still scenes.

At the end his son Sikandar stands in a procession of the unemployed, and the father must decide whether to go with the procession or stay at home. That decision comes in the last scene, so it is not being spoiled here.

The film comes to mind today because the question is the same: how someone has to prove again and again that this is their city, that they are a voter, that they are a citizen. While watching, just ask who carried the burden of answering.
nazar: This is an upload by an archive channel on YouTube, not the official channel of the rights holder. The link may be removed at some point.
The film's link to the present is our reading. The film says nothing about SIR or any law of today.
sawal: For someone told to leave his city, what does staying mean?
ref: Partition
The making of India and Pakistan in 1947, in which millions left their homes and moved across.

h: I want to be intolerable: Anne Carson and her creative process
dek: Rashmi Bhardwaj's essay on Hindwi Bela: the Nobel-winning poet calls her own poetry a failure, and finds her way in that very failure.
body: The essay opens with the point that Anne Carson herself considers her poetry a failure and wants to be 'intolerable'. Rashmi Bhardwaj reads this not as modesty but as a creative stance: poetry that goes down easily is of no use to Carson.

She lingers on Carson's construction. The fragmented form is not chance but choice, and myth is for her not old tales but a lens for seeing today. Books like 'Autobiography of Red' and 'The Beauty of the Husband' are recalled along this route.

'Nox', the elegy written for her brother, is the emotional centre of the essay. In it translation with Catullus and personal grief dissolve into each other, and the form of the book is itself like a memorial object.

In its statement for the 2026 Nobel, the Swedish Academy underlined in Carson the meeting of a philologist's passion for words and a poet's search for new meaning. The essay links this to her creative process.
nazar: The essay is a reading of Carson's statements and works, not a text of her poems. We have not taken any line of poetry here.
The author talks about Carson's creative process, so the essay opens up more for readers who have already read her books.
sawal: If a poem does not unsettle the reader, what is left of its work?
ref: Nox
Anne Carson's 2010 book, an elegy on her brother's death, published as a box of unfolding pages.
Catullus
The ancient Roman poet whose elegy on his brother's death Carson's work connects with.

h: Surrendering oneself in the dark: Hindi translation of a conversation with Anne Carson
dek: Anurag Ankur's translation on Samalochan: in a 2023 conversation with Kate Dwyer for The Paris Review, Carson speaks about being wrong, the gulf of translation and 'pause'.
body: The conversation begins with 'Wrong Norma'. Carson explains that 'Wrong' is in the title because the academic world gives you a constant fear of being declared wrong, and she wanted to loosen that mindset. For her, contradiction is a way of loosening the mind's grip.

On translation she says the space between two languages is like a gulf in which both forms float together. She considers Emily Dickinson a writer who translated herself in her own language. Even fully understanding someone she describes as like leaping into the dark.

The most interesting part is 'pause'. In the interval of searching for a word in the dictionary, the mind stayed poised on the road to knowing. The computer gives the meaning at once and this interval is lost, which she regrets.
Her simile for creating is direct: like following a fox that crossed the yard. Asked how many hours she can stay in this state, her answer was: a few minutes, if I am lucky.
nazar: This is a translation of an English conversation; the original was published in April 2024. Talk of it has grown since the Nobel, but it makes no mention of the Nobel.
In our summary Carson's answers are in our words. The full text is worth reading on Samalochan.
sawal: In an age when every answer comes at once, who will give us time to think?
ref: The Paris Review
An American literary magazine known for its long series of interviews with writers.

h: The failure of Godaan: Madan Soni's dissatisfaction
dek: Critic Madan Soni on Samalochan argues that the tragedy of Godaan is not only Hori's but also that of a novel form that sought to bind Indian life in a Western frame.
body: Ninety years after its publication, Madan Soni admits that on rereading he felt deep disappointment. According to him, Godaan has been written about with such reverence that disagreement begins to seem like 'blasphemy', whereas the life of a work is decided by whether it can bear criticism.

He grants the strength of its portrayal of peasant life: Hori's exploitation under moneylending and zamindari is recorded here as nowhere else. His complaint is about what is missing. The novel has two texts, the village one and the urban Mehta-Malti one, and the second forms no necessary relation to the first.

He also says the picture of the village is one-dimensional. It lacks culture and mythic memory, and the characters are flat and black-and-white. In this connection he recalls Renu's village and Nirmal Verma's remark that Premchand had to find some native structure for the novel.
His conclusion is that the lesson of Godaan's failure is that to this day we have not fully found the form of a truly Indian novel.
nazar: This is one critic's thesis, which does not dismiss Godaan's greatness outright. Arguments against it can also be found in the positions of Renu, Nirmal Verma and other critics.
One need not agree with the things the essay calls 'absent'. But it is necessary to raise the question.
sawal: If disagreement with a book feels like a crime, is it really alive?
ref: Godaan
Premchand's 1936 novel, the story of the peasant Hori's longing for a cow and his ruin.

h: Bhakhai akath katha birtant: Mrinal Pande begins her story
dek: The first instalment of Mrinal Pande's autobiography on Jankipul: will our readers and publishers be able to hear and bear what a woman writes, in the right context?
body: Senior writer Mrinal Pande has begun writing her story and this is the first instalment. At the start she says that when well-wishers, readers and publishers all begin to say 'now write your story', a writer feels both thrill and uncertainty.

She comes to the real meaning of the word 'vidagdha': a person who has been cooked firm in the heat of life, whereas today the word is used for a scholar. Starting from Draupadi's vidagdha mind, she asks how much generosity there is today to bear what a woman says within the discipline built by male scholars.

The title is taken from Banarasidas's 1641 autobiography 'Ardhakathanak', and in this instalment that tradition comes as a foundation. Then the difficulty of memory: without diary or notes, is it possible to weave a thin sheet by gathering shreds of the past?
The wait for further instalments is tied to this first one. This instalment is not the whole story but its preface and intent.
nazar: We wrote the summary after reading only the start of the first instalment. The rest of the autobiography has not been published yet.
The essay's style is worth reading for its native similes, which are found in the full text, not in quotation.
sawal: When a woman tells her story, who is ready to listen?
ref: Ardhakathanak
Banarasidas's autobiography written in Braj Bhasha in 1641, considered the first autobiography in Hindi.

h: Gandhi and Hermann Kallenbach's friendship: a travelogue from the Baltic coast
dek: On Samalochan, ceramic artist Sirish Saxena describes a journey through Latvia and Lithuania, where Rothko's town lies and where a statue of Gandhi's friend Kallenbach stands.
body: Sirish Saxena had gone to an international art festival in Panevezys, Lithuania. One end of the journey reaches Daugavpils in Latvia, where the painter Mark Rothko was born. The author says the art centre there is actually built in old military warehouses and barracks, and statements by Rothko are mounted on the windows of the empty buildings.
He has been to Panevezys in Lithuania three times before. This same journey took him to 'Rusne', where there is a statue of Gandhi and his friend Hermann Kallenbach.

According to the editorial note, this account is not merely a description of seeing a monument but also about the extraordinary friendship of two people and a dialogue between two cultures. We have read only the opening part of the essay.
nazar: We have not given the rest of the essay's details on the Gandhi-Kallenbach relationship here, so that nothing is said without having read it.
The purpose of a travelogue is the feel of a place more than information. Read it that way.
sawal: If art grows in an arms depot, what do we call it?
ref: Hermann Kallenbach
A close friend of Gandhi in South Africa, a German-born architect.

h: Kamini in a collage of dark desires: Pankaj Subeer's new story
dek: Published on Jankipul, this story is in a storytelling mode that has both compassion and satire. The arrival of Kammo in a colony called Phooti Bijauri sets off a stir.
body: The story begins in a colony called 'Phooti Bijauri' settled outside the city. The houses here have been bought only by those who have retired or are about to retire from government posts such as teacher, constable, lineman and clerk, that is, people who after a lifetime in crumbling government quarters have now 'come to die in a house of their own'.

One house in the colony holds three generations: grandfather, son, grandson and a woman. The story says there is no need to give their names, so they will be called just that. The story has only one name, Kamini alias Kammo.
One winter afternoon Kammo passes along the gravel road and the neighbourhood is thrown into a stir. With the help of Urdu couplets, the narrator pokes fun at people's ages and extinguished desires.
According to the editor the story is entirely in the storytelling style. We have read only its beginning, so where the story goes next is not being told here.
nazar: This summary is based on the opening of the story. We have not read the story's outcome or its text.
To give an opinion on a story without reading it fully is unfair to the story. The full text is available on Jankipul.
sawal: How does a mere footstep wake those whose desires have retired?
ref: Qissagoi
The style of telling a story as if speaking directly to the listener.

h: The Daughter I Did Not Have
dek: On 8 October, Chennai photographer K Sharad Haksar wrote this personal essay about Neha Bora. It then kept travelling on social media, and millions of people are said to have shared it.
photo_note: AI artwork by the author accompanying the essay, 'The Daughter I Did Not Have': 'Neha' made of ink, broken pencils, pellets, spectacles, a crumpled NEET paper and a lathi.
body: When I got married, I knew I wanted only one child. And in my heart, I hoped it would be a girl. I was blessed with a daughter.
The first time I held her, I made her a silent promise. You will never have to share my time. You will never have to wait for my attention. Whatever I have, you will get all of it.

I had seen families with four or five children. Parents running from morning to night, and still some child was always left waiting. I also felt our country has too many people, and nature is paying for it. One child felt right. It felt responsible.
For years, I never questioned it.
Then this year, I saw Neha Bora.

She is 29, a PhD student at JNU, a theatre artist from Khatima, a small town in the hills of Uttarakhand. When the NEET paper leak happened, she sat down at Jantar Mantar for students she did not even know. Children who had studied for years. Parents who had spent their savings on coaching and still lost.
She did not eat for 23 days.
She was 66 kilos when she started. She lost more than 7. Near the end, doctors were taking her blood three or four times a day.

The night I read that, I could not sleep. I kept seeing my own daughter in her place. On a hot Delhi road. Thin. Tired. A doctor holding her wrist again. And I knew I would not be able to stand there and watch. I would have begged her to stop.

But Neha did not stop until the work was done. And when it was over, she said her body had forgotten how to eat. It had to learn again, like a baby. Even then, still weak, she went to Bihar to meet more than 600 students who had been arrested. She did not go home to rest. She went to the ones who had stood by her.
I am a dowser. Every day I work with energy. I have learned that anger is heavy. It burns out fast. Nobody can live on anger for 23 days without food. Only love can carry you that far.
Then I read that her father was in the Army, and the family kept moving from one posting to the next.

My wife's father was also in the Army. I never call him my father-in-law. To me, he is simply Papa. My wife studied in 13 schools. Thirteen first days. Thirteen times walking into a class where nobody knew her name. Thirteen goodbyes to friends she never saw again. Army children learn to smile, pack their bags and start again. Nobody asks them how much it hurts. I see that strength in my wife every day. I saw it in Neha too.
In Ranchi, a man threw ink on her face and called her anti-national. She said she had already faced pellets and lathis in Delhi. Ink would not scare her.
Ink washes off. In energy work, we say that what people throw at you only stays if you take it in. She seems to know this without ever holding a pendulum.
Her family did not agree with her. There were fights at home. But during the hunger strike, her mother came to Jantar Mantar.

I don't know what they said to each other. I don't need to. I am a parent. I know what a mother feels when she sees her child weak and thin on a road, and still standing. Every argument is forgotten in that moment. All that is left is: this is my child.
Neha said she has not spoken to her father yet.
I don't know him. But I am a father too, and I know how hard it is for men like us to say some things out loud. So if he cannot say it yet, let me say it for him, from Chennai.
Beta, we are proud of you. Now go and eat something properly.
Somewhere in all this, a thought came to me that I never expected. I wish I had one more daughter. One like Neha.
This takes nothing away from my own daughter. She is my world. She always will be.

But Neha made me ask myself a hard question. We spend our whole lives keeping our children safe and helping them get ahead. Do we ever teach them to look back at who is being left behind? And if one day they stand up for someone else, will we stand next to them as Neha's mother did? Or will we ask them to come home and stay quiet?
I believe every child is born with a spark of the Divine. Our job is to protect that light, even when it scares us.
I wanted one daughter, and I was blessed with her.
Tonight I will call her. Not for anything. Just to hear her voice.
And I will think of another girl, somewhere in Delhi, learning to eat again.
nazar: This is a personal essay by a father and artist, not a report. The details of Neha Bora's fast, the Ranchi incident and her mother's visit to Jantar Mantar are taken by the author from media reports; Deshkaal has not separately verified them independently.
'Dowsing' is a method that claims to find energy or water with a pendulum or rod, and it has no scientific recognition. The essay's emotional capital comes not from that but from its question.
The claim of millions of shares was told to us. Deshkaal has not made an independent count of the shares.
sawal: If our children stand up for someone else, will we stand beside them?
ref: K Sharad Haksar
A Chennai photographer and creative director. According to his own profile, a Cannes Silver Lion winner and founder of OneEyeland.com.
Dowsing
A method that claims to find energy or water with the help of a pendulum or rod.
intro: Today Sadak ki Sansad has six essays: on the Commission, the court, the police and politics. This one is not among those six, because it is not anyone's analysis but a father's restlessness at night.

K Sharad Haksar wrote it in English on 8 October. After that the essay began to travel on its own: from WhatsApp to feeds, from one phone to another. It is said that millions of people shared it. No slogan, no statistic, just the father of a daughter and another daughter who sat hungry for 23 days at Jantar Mantar. Below is the full essay in English.

h: Khamri village: after displacement the forest is 15-20 km away, livelihood from amla and mahua lost
dek: A short ground report by Khabar Lahariya from Panna (Madhya Pradesh): villagers can no longer easily reach the forest that gave them amla, mahua, charva and tendu leaves in October.
body: People of Khamri village in Gunaur block of Panna district say that after displacement both their dependence on the forest and their livelihood have been affected.
According to the villagers, from October, along with picking amla, the forest gave produce such as mahua, charva and tendu leaves. After displacement they have been cut off from their old forest.
They say the forest is now about 15-20 km from Khamri village and getting there is also difficult.
nazar: This is a very short Khabar Lahariya report resting on what villagers say. It does not say why or when the displacement happened, what the position on compensation or rehabilitation is, and what the administration's side is.
sawal: When people whose livelihood ran on the forest are settled away from it, who keeps the account of their work?
ref: Mahua
A tree whose flowers and fruit are used in villages for food and sale.
Tendu leaf
The leaf used for making beedis, plucked from the forest and sold.
